levels.title: Crate Sorter
levels.story: On Brute Bay the harbour is stacked with crates in no order at all. Kit gets the first honest method: no cleverness, just do the obvious thing, and then count what it costs.

everyday.scene: You have a shuffled pile of exam papers to put in order by score. Without thinking much, you pick out the lowest, put it on the left, pick out the lowest of what remains, and so on.
everyday.question: Is that a method a computer could follow?
everyday.answer: Yes. It is called selection sort, and it is a good example of brute force: the straightforward plan that comes to mind first. It costs n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons, which is 15 for 6 papers.

lessons.title: Brute force: the first plan
text: Brute force means solving a problem in the most direct way the wording suggests, without clever shortcuts. It is easy to explain, easy to get right, and it is a fair baseline: if a smarter method cannot beat it, there is no point using it.

Its weakness is cost. Direct methods often do far more work than needed. In Algo Archipelago you will use brute force as the first draft, then count its steps to see whether a better one is worth finding.

terms.meaning: The most direct method, often trying everything.
A simple method used as the standard to beat.

predict.prompt: Name one everyday job where you would just try everything.
predict.answer: For example, finding a lost key by checking every pocket and drawer. It always works, and it is slow only if there are lots of places.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 0: Introduction

lessons.title: Selection sort
text: Selection sort keeps a sorted part at the left and an unsorted part at the right. Each pass scans the unsorted part to find its smallest crate, then swaps it into the first unsorted spot. After n − 1 passes everything is in order.
Pass 1 compares n − 1 times, pass 2 compares n − 2 times, and so on. That adds up to n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons, whatever order the crates started in. It also makes at most one swap per pass.

terms.meaning: One sweep through the unsorted part.

predict.prompt: Selection sort runs on 5 crates. How many comparisons?

lessons.title: Bubble sort
text: Bubble sort sweeps along the row and compares each neighbouring pair, swapping them if they are the wrong way round. The biggest crate drifts to the end each sweep, like a bubble rising. After n − 1 sweeps the row is sorted.

The plain version compares n − 1 pairs on the first sweep, n − 2 on the next, and so on: again n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons. Swaps are different. A reversed row needs a swap at every comparison, while a sorted row needs none.

predict.prompt: Which does more swapping in bubble sort: a sorted row or a reversed row?
predict.answer: A reversed row. Every pair is the wrong way round.

deeper.title: Stopping early
text: A common improvement stops when a whole sweep makes no swap. That helps on rows that are nearly sorted. It does not change the worst case.

fieldNotes.title: Sorting by hand, at small scale
fieldNotes.text: Simple sorts like selection and insertion sort are fine for short lists. Many faster sorts split a list into pieces and switch to a simple method such as insertion sort once the pieces are small, because the extra bookkeeping of the clever method does not pay off at small sizes.

summary: You watched selection sort pick the smallest crate each pass, counted its comparisons as n × (n − 1) ÷ 2, and compared it with bubble sort.
The harbour is tidy. "It works," says the harbour master. "But look how the count grows. Keep that in mind for the next islands."

mistake.title: Thinking fewer swaps means less work
mistake.text: Selection sort makes few swaps but still makes n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons. Always say what you are counting: comparisons or swaps.

levels.title: Message in a Bottle
levels.story: A bottle washes up with a long scrawl inside, and the islanders want to know whether the word they are afraid of is in it. Kit slides the word along the message, one place at a time.

everyday.scene: You press Ctrl+F in a long web page to find a word. Somewhere, a program has to look through the text for it.
everyday.question: What is the simplest way for it to look?
everyday.answer: Line the word up at the start, check letter by letter, and if a letter differs, slide the word one place along and try again. That is brute-force string matching, and it is simple enough to write in a few lines.

lessons.title: Slide and compare
text: Brute-force string matching lines the pattern up under the start of the text and compares letter by letter. If every letter matches, you have found it. At the first letter that differs, you stop, slide the pattern one place to the right, and begin again.
With a text of 11 letters and a pattern of 7, there are 11 − 7 + 1 = 5 places to try. In our example, it found a match at position 4, after 14 letter comparisons in total.

terms.meaning: The word or string you are looking for.
The long string you search inside.

predict.prompt: A text has 20 letters, and the pattern has 5. How many placements are there?

lessons.title: The worst case
text: Most placements fail fast: the first letter is often wrong, so one comparison is enough. The worst case is when the pattern nearly matches everywhere. Searching for AAAB in AAAAAAAAAA, every placement matches three letters before the B fails.

With n letters of text and m letters in the pattern, the worst case is about (n − m + 1) × m comparisons. For n = 10 and m = 4 that is 28. The best case, where the first letter always fails, is just n − m + 1.

predict.prompt: Which is slower to search: a pattern of 10 A's in a long text of A's, or a pattern starting with a letter the text never contains?
predict.answer: The A's. The other fails at the first letter at every placement.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 0: Introduction

lessons.title: Why people look for better ways
text: For short patterns on everyday text, brute force is fast enough. Real text is not like the worst case, and most placements fail at once. So brute force is a respectable method for small jobs.

But the worst case matters when the text is huge or when someone chooses the input on purpose. Later, in Trade Wind Cove, you will meet methods that skip ahead after a mismatch and so avoid re-reading letters.

predict.prompt: Why is brute force acceptable for most everyday searches?
predict.answer: Most placements fail on the first letter, so the average is close to the best case.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 0: Introduction

fieldNotes.title: Find in page
fieldNotes.text: Finding a short piece of text inside a long one is called string searching. The simple method, trying every starting position, is often fine for short patterns, because on ordinary text a wrong position is usually spotted after one or two characters.

summary: You slid a pattern along a text, counted letter comparisons, and met the worst case (n − m + 1) × m.
The islanders relax. "Our word is not in the bottle." Brute force found the answer, and it told you how much it cost.

mistake.title: Forgetting to stop at the first mismatch
mistake.text: Brute force stops comparing as soon as one letter differs, then slides on. Counting all m letters at every placement overstates the work except in the worst case.

levels.title: Closest Lighthouses
levels.story: Two lighthouses are so close that their beams clash. Captain Ada wants to know which pair, and the chart has dozens of them. Kit measures them all.

everyday.scene: Your phone shows 40 friends on a map, and you want to find the two who live closest to each other.
everyday.question: How many pairs of friends is that to check?
everyday.answer: Every friend against every other: 40 × 39 ÷ 2 = 780 pairs. That is the brute-force plan for the closest-pair problem, and it is fine for 40. It is slow for 4 million.

lessons.title: Measure every pair
text: The closest-pair problem: given points on a map, find the two that are nearest to each other. Brute force measures every pair, remembers the smallest distance so far, and reports the best at the end.
With n points there are n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 pairs. For 8 points that is 28, for 1,000 it is 499,500, and for a million it is nearly 500 billion. The plan is correct, and its cost grows like n × n.

terms.meaning: Two different points, counted once whichever order you name them.

predict.prompt: How many pairs can you form from 6 lighthouses?

references.title: Wikipedia: Closest pair of points problem

lessons.title: Skip the square root
text: The distance between points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is the square root of (x1 − x2)² + (y1 − y2)². But we only need to find which pair is closest, and the biggest-or-smallest order does not change if we skip the square root.

So compare squared distances instead. For (3,4) and (9,12), the squared distance is 100, so the real distance is 10. Squaring costs less than a square root, and in a loop that runs half a million times, it adds up.

predict.prompt: Which is smaller: squared distance 25 or squared distance 36?
predict.answer: 25. The real distances are 5 and 6, and the order is the same.

deeper.title: Why the order stays the same
text: Squaring keeps order for numbers that are zero or bigger. A distance is never negative, so a smaller squared distance always means a smaller distance.

references.title: Wikipedia: Closest pair of points problem

lessons.title: Keep the best so far
text: The loop remembers one thing: the best pair so far and its squared distance. For each new pair, it measures, compares, and only replaces the best if the new pair is strictly closer.
It never needs to store all the distances, only the best. That small habit, keeping a running best, appears in many brute-force searches, including finding the biggest crate in the first island.

predict.prompt: What does the loop need to remember between pairs?
predict.answer: The best pair so far and its squared distance.

references.title: Wikipedia: Closest pair of points problem
Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 0: Introduction

fieldNotes.title: Nearest neighbour searches
fieldNotes.text: Finding the nearest point to a given spot, or the closest pair, comes up in map apps and in graphics. For small sets, checking every pair is enough. For big sets, faster methods exist, and you will meet one on Split Rock.

source.title: Wikipedia: Closest pair of points problem

summary: You measured every pair of lighthouses, compared squared distances and kept the best so far. The cost is n × (n − 1) ÷ 2.
Ada marks the chart. "Two beams clash, and now we know which." A smarter plan for huge charts waits on Split Rock.

mistake.title: Counting pairs twice
mistake.text: The pair A–B and the pair B–A are the same pair. Counting both gives n × (n − 1), double the real number.

levels.title: Island Tour & Treasure Bag
levels.story: Fen wants one tour that visits every island exactly once, and Pia wants to fill a bag with the most valuable treasure. Both problems have a perfectly good brute-force answer, and both explode with size.

everyday.scene: You have six errands to run across town, and you want the shortest trip that visits each place once and gets you home.
everyday.question: How many different orders could you try?
everyday.answer: For 6 stops there are 60 different round trips. For 20 stops there are about 60 quadrillion. Trying them all is correct, and quickly hopeless.

lessons.title: The island tour
text: The travelling salesman problem asks for the shortest round trip that visits every town once and returns to the start. Brute force tries every order and keeps the shortest.

Fix the starting town. The other n − 1 towns can be visited in (n − 1)! orders. A tour and its reverse have the same length, so there are (n − 1)! ÷ 2 different tours. That is 12 for 5 towns, 60 for 6 and 181,440 for 10.

predict.prompt: A salesman visits 4 towns and returns home. How many different tours are there?

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 2: Backtracking

lessons.title: The treasure bag
text: The knapsack problem: each treasure has a weight and a value, the bag holds a fixed weight, and you want the highest total value that fits. Brute force tries every subset of the treasures.
Each treasure is either in or out, so n treasures make 2 × 2 × … × 2 = 2ⁿ subsets: 16 for 4 treasures, 1,024 for 10, and 1,073,741,824 for 30. Each subset is checked by adding up weights and values.

predict.prompt: A bag could hold any of 5 treasures. How many different subsets are there?
predict.answer: 32. Each treasure is in or out: 2⁵ = 32.

lessons.title: When brute force explodes
text: Both problems fall off a cliff. At a billion tours per second, 20 towns need about 1.9 years. Adding one more town multiplies the work by 20. Adding one treasure doubles the subset count.

Brute force is still the right first draft, and for small n it is fine. But these growth rates (factorial and exponential) are the reason that smarter methods, and ways of settling for a good-enough answer, exist.

predict.prompt: What happens to the number of subsets when you add one more treasure?

deeper.title: Is there a trick?
text: For both problems, no method is known that is fast for every input, and many experts believe none exists. You will meet this idea again in the P versus NP topic.

fieldNotes.title: Delivery routes
fieldNotes.text: Planning delivery routes is known as the vehicle routing problem, and it is NP-hard. Because of that, many real applications do not try every order. They use methods that quickly build a relatively good route, even if it is not provably the best one.

summary: You counted tours with (n − 1)! ÷ 2 and treasure subsets with 2ⁿ, and found the best bag by trying every subset.
Fen sighs at the 60 quadrillion. "So no, I will not try them all." Knowing a method will not scale is as useful as knowing it works.

mistake.title: Calling both growth rates "just very big"
mistake.text: Factorial and 2ⁿ are both explosive, but factorial is far worse: 20! is about 2.4 quintillion, while 2²⁰ is about a million.

levels.title: Bridge Walker
levels.story: The mayor of the isles wants a parade that crosses every bridge exactly once. Kit tries every possible walk, then discovers a shortcut that answers the question without walking at all.

everyday.scene: You are a postman, and you want a route that walks along every street once and never repeats a street.
everyday.question: Do you have to try every possible route to know whether one exists?
everyday.answer: You could, but a famous 18th-century trick lets you answer by counting how many junctions have an odd number of streets.

lessons.title: Try every walk
text: Exhaustive search tries every possibility, but extends partial answers step by step and backs up when stuck. To find a walk over all bridges, start on an island, cross an unused bridge, and keep going. If you run out of bridges before finishing, back up and try another bridge.

For our five bridges, the search finds 12 walks that cross each bridge exactly once, counting different starting islands and directions separately. But it has to try partial walks that fail along the way, and on bigger maps the number of walks explodes.

terms.meaning: Trying all possibilities, one by one, until you find what you need or run out.
Undoing the last step and trying a different option when you are stuck.

predict.prompt: Kit crosses a bridge and finds no unused bridge, but some are left. What does exhaustive search do?
predict.answer: It backs up one step and tries a different bridge.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 2: Backtracking

lessons.title: Counting bridges
text: A bridge count is called an island's degree. Euler noticed that on a walk that crosses every bridge once, every island you pass through is entered and left, using bridges in pairs. So an island in the middle of the walk must have an even degree.

Only the starting and ending islands can have an odd degree. So a connected map has a walk over every bridge exactly once only if it has 0 or 2 islands with an odd degree. Count the degrees, and you have your answer.

terms.meaning: The number of bridges at an island.
A degree of 1, 3, 5 and so on.

predict.prompt: A map has 4 islands with an odd degree. Can you cross every bridge once?
predict.answer: No. Only 0 or 2 odd islands allowed.

lessons.title: Counting beats walking
text: Counting degrees takes one look at each island, while exhaustive search may try thousands of walks. For our map: with only 12 successful walks hidden among many partial ones, the count is much faster.

This is a good habit: before searching, ask whether a property of the problem rules answers in or out. Not every problem has such a shortcut, but when one does, it can turn an impossible search into a glance.

predict.prompt: Why is counting odd islands faster than searching?
predict.answer: It looks at each island once, instead of trying many walks.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 2: Backtracking

activities.prompt: In the five-bridge map (bridges A–B, B–C, C–D, D–A and A–C), how many bridges are at island A?
hints: Count the bridges that touch A.
A–B, D–A and A–C.
activities.explain: A has three bridges: A–B, D–A and A–C.

activities.prompt: How many of the four islands have an odd number of bridges?
hints: A has 3 and C has 3. What about B and D?
B and D have 2 each.
activities.explain: A and C have 3, and B and D have 2, so 2 islands are odd. That means a walk exists, starting at one odd island and ending at the other.

activities.prompt: A different map has islands P, Q, R, S and T and bridges P–Q, Q–R, R–S, S–P, P–R and S–T. Can a walk cross every bridge exactly once?

options.text: No: four islands have an odd number of bridges
Yes: it has fewer than ten bridges
Yes: any connected map works
No: it has more than five bridges

hints: Count the bridges at each island.
P, R and S have 3 each, T has 1, and Q has 2.
activities.explain: P, R, S and T all have an odd degree: 4 odd islands, and a walk needs 0 or 2.

activities.prompt: Put exhaustive search for a bridge walk in order.
items: Check whether every bridge has been crossed
If stuck, back up one step
hints: The check for finishing comes after crossing a bridge.
You only back up when you are stuck.
activities.explain: Start, cross, check, back up if stuck, try another bridge.

activities.prompt: Challenge: five bridges can be crossed in 5! different orders if you ignore whether the order is a real walk. How many orders is that?
activities.explain: 5! = 120. Most of these orders are not real walks, but a very simple search would still try them.

activities.prompt: Challenge: exhaustive search on the five-bridge map finds how many successful walks in total (counting each starting island and each direction separately)?
hints: Walks must start at A or C, the two odd islands.
Each walk and its reverse both count.
activities.explain: The search finds 12 walks. ABCDAC, ABCADC, ADCBAC, ADCABC and others, each starting on A or C.

fieldNotes.title: Euler and the bridges of Königsberg
fieldNotes.text: The idea behind this level goes back to 1736, when Leonhard Euler showed that the seven bridges of the city of Königsberg could not all be crossed once in a single walk. His proof laid the foundations of graph theory.

summary: You watched a walk cross every bridge, saw how exhaustive search backs up when stuck, and learned that counting odd-degree islands answers the question at a glance.
The mayor cheers. "A parade with no repeats." Sometimes a bit of thinking replaces a mountain of searching.

mistake.title: Forgetting that the map must be connected
mistake.text: The odd-island rule works for maps where every island can be reached from the others. Two separate groups of islands can never share one walk.
